  "text": "A researcher’s approach for examining shrub plants in grazing areas was adopted by a land‑management agency to study browse species on winter wildlife ranges in a western region. Small sample plots were set up and records kept of how much browse was eaten, while grasses were noted only for their abundance because they were barely used. So far only grazed and protected plots have been examined, but plans call for additional plots with removable barriers to test how different grazing pressures affect plant health and forage production. Knowing the safe consumption level of the main browse plants is crucial for wildlife management, since the winter range’s carrying capacity limits animal numbers. Studying use intensity where animal counts are known can provide an index for areas lacking reliable censuses.
